strengths: Provides the first systematic, unified framework encompassing a wide range of existing attentive probing/pooling methods (AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA, CLIP, SigLIP, CoCa, CAiT, CAE, CBAM), clearly deriving each as a special case of a common MHCA formulation, which is a valuable conceptual contribution.

The proposed Efficient Probing (EP) method is simple, well-motivated (removal of redundant key projections by absorbing them into learnable queries), and is theoretically justified with a clear derivation, and connects EP to slot attention conceptually.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 4 MIM backbones (MAE, SimMIM, BEiTv2, CAPI), multiple backbone sizes (ViT-S/B/L), 7+ classification benchmarks, and additional joint-embedding/hybrid/vision-language pretraining methods, showing consistent Pareto-optimal accuracy-parameter and accuracy-FLOPs trade-offs.
Thorough ablations (impact of W_K, W_V, number of heads/queries, output dimensionality) that support the design choices with clear, interpretable trends.
Interesting analysis correlating attention localization quality/entropy with classification contribution, providing some interpretability insight beyond raw accuracy numbers.

Additional experiments (layer-wise probing, low-shot probing) strengthen the case that EP is a practically useful drop-in replacement for LP, and attention visualizations (Figs 6, 10-13) qualitatively support claims of complementary, interpretable per-query attention maps.
Reasonably strong writing and organization, with a comprehensive supplementary material including additional related work (PEFT) and further experiments.
weaknesses: The central technical contribution (removing W_K by absorbing it into a learnable query) is an incremental simplification of existing MHCA-based probing mechanisms already in the literature (AbMILP being nearly identical with M=1); the novelty is somewhat narrow in scope even though the benchmark contribution is broader.

No standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere for the reported accuracies, especially given many results differ by <1%, e.g., between EP and closest competitors (e.g., AIM, CAE) — makes it hard to assess statistical significance of claimed 'state-of-the-art' or 'consistently outperforms' statements.

The paper's plots (Figures 3, 9) are dense and somewhat difficult to parse quantitatively; exact numeric tables for the main comparisons (beyond Table 1) are largely relegated to figures rather than tables, making precise comparison and reproducibility harder for readers.

The correlation analysis between localization quality/entropy and accuracy (Figure 5, Section 4.4) is presented somewhat informally, without a quantitative correlation coefficient or statistical test, weakening claims of a 'strong correlation.'

Comparisons to full fine-tuning (Table 1) show EP/LP still noticeably lag FT in most cases (e.g., MAE FT 83.6 vs. EP not explicitly listed in table, though claimed elsewhere it's competitive) — the practical significance of closing the FT gap could be stated more precisely and consistently across the paper.
Limited discussion of computational/training cost trade-offs beyond FLOPs for the probe itself; wall-clock training/inference time comparisons are not provided.

The paper's scope, while broad, is confined to image classification benchmarks; it does not explore probing for other downstream tasks (e.g., segmentation, detection) where localization quality claims would be more directly testable.

strengths: Provides a genuinely useful unifying framework that recasts many existing attentive probing/pooling methods (AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA, CLIP, SigLIP, CoCa, CaiT) as special cases of a single generic MHCA formulation, which is a nice conceptual contribution for organizing a fragmented literature.

The proposed Efficient Probing (EP) method is simple to implement and yields substantial parameter and FLOPs reductions (up to 10x fewer compute vs. vanilla MHCA, ~4x fewer parameters than linear probing) while matching or exceeding accuracy of more complex baselines.

Very extensive empirical study: 7 classification benchmarks, 4 MIM pretraining methods, multiple backbone sizes (ViT-S/B/L), low-shot regime, layer-wise probing, and several ablations (W_K, W_V, number of heads/queries, output dimensionality) — much more thorough than most probing papers.

The localization-quality vs. classification-accuracy correlation analysis (Figure 5) and the attention map visualizations (Figures 6, 10-13) give some interpretability insight and support the claim that EP produces complementary, object-focused attention.

Generalization experiments beyond MIM (to JEA, hybrid, and vision-language models) and the Pareto-frontier framing (accuracy vs. parameters vs. FLOPs) are informative for practitioners choosing a probing method.
weaknesses: The core novelty is incremental: EP is essentially an engineering simplification of existing attentive-pooling/MHCA designs (removing the key projection and query projection, replacing them with directly learnable query vectors), closely related to AbMILP generalized to M queries; the conceptual leap over prior art is modest for a top-tier venue.

There is an internal tension in the paper's own ablation: Section 4.6 shows that removing W_K in multi-head attention (AIM) causes a noticeable accuracy drop (75.1%→72.9%), yet EP removes W_K entirely and still claims SOTA performance; the paper does not clearly reconcile why EP's learnable-query trick avoids this degradation, leaving the central efficiency claim under-justified mechanistically.

Figures 3 and 9 are extremely dense and visually cluttered with many overlapping colored points and method labels, making it hard to verify specific accuracy/parameter claims at a glance; no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere, so the statistical significance of small accuracy differences (often <1%) between EP and competing methods is unclear.

Evaluation is restricted entirely to image classification; given that attentive probing is motivated by MIM's distributed, spatially-localized representations, downstream tasks such as segmentation or detection (where localization quality matters more directly) would be a more convincing testbed and are absent.

The paper reports fine-tuning (FT) numbers only from the literature (Table 1) rather than evaluating EP itself in an FT setting or discussing more rigorously how close attentive probing comes to closing the FT gap, limiting the practical significance of the 'probing as FT alternative' narrative.

The method/hyperparameter search (learning rate range, epoch count, batch sizes) is not thoroughly justified for every competitor, raising concerns about whether some baselines are under-tuned relative to EP, which could bias the reported Pareto-frontier comparisons in EP's favor.

Experiments are confined to ViT backbones pretrained with a specific set of MIM/JEA methods; no evaluation on larger-scale or more modern self-supervised backbones (e.g., ViT-H/g, DINOv2-giant) is included, limiting evidence of scalability of the method to the regime where probing is most needed in practice.

strengths: Provides the first systematic, unified framework that recasts many existing attentive-pooling/probing methods (AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA, CLIP, CAiT, SigLIP, CoCa, CBAM) as instances of a common multi-head cross-attention formulation, clarifying their design differences and parameter/compute trade-offs.

Proposes Efficient Probing (EP), a simple multi-query cross-attention mechanism that removes redundant key/query projections, yielding large parameter and FLOP savings while matching or exceeding the accuracy of more heavily parameterized attentive probing baselines.

Extremely broad empirical evaluation: 15 pre-training methods across MIM, JEA, hybrid, VLM, and generative paradigms, 7+ datasets (ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-100, Places365, FGVC-Aircraft, Stanford Cars, CUB-200, Food-101), multiple backbone sizes, plus layer-wise and low-shot probing analyses.

Interesting and non-trivial analysis connecting attention localization quality/entropy to downstream classification contribution, and a novel complementarity metric showing that EP's learned queries specialize into diverse, interpretable, and less redundant regions than internal self-attention heads or competing probes.

Thorough ablations (impact of W_K/W_V, number of queries/output dimension, attention mixing, Matryoshka-style multi-scale probing) and rich qualitative visualizations that support the quantitative claims.
Good positioning within PEFT literature and clear, well-organized appendix covering additional methods, datasets, and limitations.
weaknesses: The core method (EP) is largely a simplification/pruning of existing MHCA-based attentive pooling (removing key/value projections, using learnable queries directly in input space), and its conceptual novelty is modest; the paper itself notes its close relationship to AbMILP and slot attention.

Accuracy gains over strong existing attentive probing baselines (AIM, MHCA, CAE, CLIP-style pooling) are often marginal in absolute top-1 accuracy (Figures 2-3, Table 2); the main advantage is parameter/FLOP efficiency rather than a clear accuracy improvement, which somewhat tempers claims of "state-of-the-art accuracy."

All evaluation is restricted to image classification; despite the paper's emphasis on localization quality and part-level attention as a key finding, there is no evaluation on tasks that would directly benefit from and validate this property (e.g., detection, segmentation, retrieval), leaving the practical significance of the localization/complementarity findings only indirectly supported.

No fine-tuning or PEFT-adapter comparisons are run under the same experimental protocol (FT numbers are only quoted from original papers under different training conditions), making the framing relative to "fine-tuning being impractical" only partially substantiated experimentally.

There is no indication of results being averaged over multiple seeds or reporting variance, which is important given the fine-grained accuracy differences (often <1%) used to rank many closely competing pooling methods.

The learning-rate search and training protocol (LARS, per-model tuning) could favor certain methods; it is unclear whether all baselines (especially heavier ones like CAiT, SigLIP-style poolers) received comparably exhaustive tuning, raising a minor fairness concern in the comparisons.

The paper is very dense with many metrics, ablations, and figures spread across a long appendix, which, while thorough, makes the core contribution and its significance somewhat diffuse and harder to assess at a glance.

strengths: Presents a genuinely comprehensive unified framework that recasts many existing attentive pooling/probing methods (AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA, CLIP, CAiT, SigLIP, CoCa, CAE, etc.) as instances of a common multi-head cross-attention formulation, which is a useful organizing contribution for the field.

Very extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple pre-training paradigms (MIM, JEA, hybrid, VLM, generative/autoregressive), backbone sizes (ViT-S/B/L, DiT-XL), and seven downstream datasets, which is more thorough than most prior probing papers.

The proposed Efficient Probing (EP) mechanism is a clean, well-motivated simplification (removing redundant query/key projections, using directly learnable multi-query vectors) with clear reductions in parameter count and FLOPs, and the derivation logically follows from the paper's own ablations (e.g., single-head query absorption argument).

Rich set of secondary analyses (layer-wise probing, low-shot probing, attention complementarity metrics, entropy vs. accuracy correlation, Matryoshka representation learning, attention mixing, extensive qualitative visualizations) that go beyond simple accuracy tables and offer some interpretability insight.
Reasonable reproducibility support via detailed appendix describing datasets, optimizer, learning-rate search protocol, and compute infrastructure.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (EP) is a fairly small architectural simplification—removing the key projection and using directly learnable query vectors—rather than a conceptually novel idea; its derivation and connection to slot attention is straightforward and incremental despite the paper's framing as a major contribution.

Reported accuracy gains of EP over competitive baselines (AIM, MHCA, CAE, CLIP) at matched parameter counts are often marginal (e.g., Figure 2, Figure 8), and the Pareto-frontier argument relies heavily on cherry-picked operating points (varying D_o) rather than uniformly dominant performance.

No indication of statistical robustness: results appear to be single-run numbers without error bars, variance across seeds, or significance testing, which is concerning given some reported gains are small (fractions of a percent) relative to likely run-to-run variance in probing.

The extensive per-model learning-rate search (performed presumably for every pooling method, including EP) raises fairness/tuning-effort concerns — it is unclear whether all competitor methods received equally thorough hyperparameter search, which could bias comparisons in EP's favor.

The paper is essentially a large-scale benchmarking/evaluation-protocol study; while thorough, its overall scientific novelty and impact are narrower than a new representation-learning or architectural contribution, and the central claims (attentive probing better reflects patch-distributed representations, complementary attention improves interpretability) largely confirm intuitions already suggested in cited prior work (AIM, V-JEPA, Darcet et al. 2025) rather than establishing fundamentally new understanding.

The complementarity metric and localization-vs-accuracy correlation analyses are purely correlational/diagnostic without causal validation (e.g., no experiment that explicitly optimizes for complementarity to demonstrate it is a driver rather than a byproduct of EP's design), weakening the strength of the interpretability claims.

Figures are extremely dense (many small multi-panel plots with numerous overlapping colored points/labels), making it difficult to visually verify claimed Pareto-optimality or trends, which hurts clarity and reviewer/reader ability to independently verify central claims.

Fine-tuning remains substantially better than EP in most settings (Table 2), and the low-shot gap-closing metric, while positive, still leaves a meaningful gap to FT, somewhat undercutting the framing that probing is a full substitute for fine-tuning.

strengths: Provides the first systematic, unified benchmark of attentive probing methods, recasting many prior heterogeneous designs (AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA, CLIP, SigLIP, CaiT, CoCa, CAE, etc.) into a common multi-head cross-attention framework, enabling principled apples-to-apples comparison.

The proposed Efficient Probing (EP) method is derived through a clear, well-motivated ablation chain (showing that key projections can be absorbed into a learnable query and are largely redundant), resulting in a simple, parameter- and compute-efficient design that is easy to reproduce.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 15 pre-training methods spanning five paradigms (MIM, JEA, hybrid, VLM, generative/AR) and 7 datasets of varying scale and granularity (ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-100, Places365, FGVC-Aircraft, Stanford Cars, CUB-200, Food-101), with consistent Pareto-frontier analysis of accuracy vs. parameters and accuracy vs. FLOPs.

Goes beyond raw accuracy to provide interesting analyses: correlation between attention localization quality/entropy and classification contribution, layer-wise probing robustness, low-shot probing, Matryoshka-style multi-scale probing, and a novel 'attention complementarity' metric showing EP's queries specialize in diverse, interpretable object regions.

Strong, consistent empirical gains: EP matches or exceeds prior attentive probing/pooling methods while using substantially fewer parameters and FLOPs, and narrows the gap to full fine-tuning (e.g., closing 71-75% of the LP→FT gap in low-shot settings, +24.3% top-1 gain on DiT).

Good reproducibility support: detailed appendix describing additional baseline methods, implementation/hyperparameter details, datasets, and compute resources, plus qualitative attention visualizations that substantiate the interpretability claims.
weaknesses: All experiments are restricted to image classification; the paper's claims about attentive probing's advantage for localizing/part-based information are not validated on tasks that directly require spatial reasoning (e.g., detection, segmentation, retrieval), which are mentioned only as future work.

The complementarity and entropy/localization analyses are correlational/diagnostic rather than causal or theoretically grounded; no controlled intervention isolates whether complementarity itself (vs. other confounds like effective capacity) drives the accuracy gains.

No reported variance or multiple-seed results/error bars for the many accuracy comparisons, making it hard to judge whether some reported gaps (e.g., EP vs. AIM/MHCA/V-JEPA at similar parameter counts, which are sometimes within a fraction of a point) are statistically meaningful.

The core methodological novelty of EP is somewhat incremental — it is essentially MHCA with the key projection removed and queries learned directly in feature space — though the surrounding unified framework and systematic study add value beyond the method alone.

A uniform training/optimization recipe (LARS, fixed epoch budget, per-model LR sweep) is applied across very heterogeneous pre-training paradigms (SSL, VLM, diffusion, autoregressive); some baselines (e.g., CLIP/SigLIP with their typical fine-tuning recipes) might be sensitive to this choice, raising some concern about full fairness of the comparison, though the authors do control for this reasonably well.

Several additional contributions (attention mixing, Matryoshka probing) are explored only briefly in the appendix without deep analysis of when/why they help or fail, leaving these avenues underdeveloped relative to the main EP contribution.

strengths: Presents a unified, mathematically grounded framework that recasts a wide range of existing attentive probing/pooling methods (AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA, CLIP, CAiT, SigLIP, CoCa, etc.) as instances of a common multi-head/multi-query cross-attention formulation, which is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution beyond the proposed method itself.

The proposed Efficient Probing (EP) mechanism is simple, well-motivated by a clear derivation (removing redundant W_K via mathematical equivalence arguments), and is shown both analytically and empirically to reduce parameters/FLOPs substantially while matching or exceeding accuracy.

Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: multiple pre-training paradigms (MIM, JEA, hybrid, VLM, generative/diffusion, autoregressive), many backbones and model sizes, 7+ datasets, layer-wise probing, low-shot probing, cross-dataset k-NN, WSOL localization, zero-shot retrieval, and PEFT comparisons (LoRA/BitFit/LayerNorm) with hybrid LoRA+EP configurations that dominate both pure approaches.

Interesting and non-trivial analysis linking attention localization quality to classification accuracy gains, and introduction of a complementarity metric showing EP's queries specialize into diverse, interpretable, semantically meaningful regions compared to internal MHSA heads and other probing methods.

Extensive ablations (impact of W_K/W_V, entropy analysis, query count/output dimension sweeps, attention mixing, Matryoshka representation probing, EP convergence speed) that go well beyond what is typical, demonstrating robustness of the central claims.
Good scholarly hygiene: honest limitations section, LLM usage disclosure, extensive appendix reproducing many additional experiments and visualizations that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution (EP) is an incremental simplification of existing MHCA-with-learnable-query designs (removing W_K by absorbing it into learnable queries) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; novelty is somewhat modest even though the empirical execution is strong.

Some plots (e.g., Figure 2, Figure 9) are visually dense and hard to parse with many overlapping labeled points, making it difficult for readers to precisely verify claimed Pareto dominance from the figures alone; more explicit tabulated head-to-head comparisons at matched parameter budgets would strengthen clarity.

The complementarity metric, while interesting, is somewhat ad hoc (cosine similarity based diversity measure) and its causal link to downstream accuracy/interpretability is only correlational; the paper acknowledges this as diagnostic rather than theoretically grounded, leaving the significance of the 'complementarity' finding a bit speculative.

All experiments use frozen backbones with a full forward pass each step; the more practical frozen-feature caching setting is left entirely to future work, which somewhat limits the immediate practical efficiency story despite the parameter efficiency emphasis.

The paper compares to PEFT methods mainly through LoRA/BitFit/LayerNorm on a single backbone (MAE ViT-B/16) for the PEFT comparison in Fig. 4/Section 4.2's PEFT paragraph, limiting generality of the PEFT-related conclusions relative to the breadth of the rest of the paper.

Given the very large number of experiments, statistical significance (e.g., variance across seeds) is not discussed, so some of the smaller reported gains (e.g., sub-1% accuracy differences in some tables) may not be robustly distinguishable from noise.

strengths: Very extensive empirical study spanning many pre-training paradigms (MIM, JEA, hybrid, VLM, AR, diffusion), multiple backbone sizes, and seven downstream datasets, which gives the benchmark broad coverage.

The unified mathematical framework (Table 1) that recasts existing attentive probing/pooling methods (AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA, CLIP, CAiT, SigLIP, CoCa, CAE) as special cases of a common multi-head/multi-query cross-attention formulation is a useful organizing contribution and clarifies design choices across a fragmented literature.

The derivation of EP is logically motivated: starting from MHCA, the paper shows analytically that absorbing the key projection into the learnable query removes redundant parameters without theoretical loss of expressiveness (when M=1), and empirically explores the cost of doing so for M>1.

Thorough appendix with many additional experiments: low-shot probing, in/out-of-domain k-NN, object localization (MaxBoxAccV2), zero-shot retrieval, layer-wise probing, Matryoshka-style multi-scale probing, convergence speed, and attention-mixing ablations, which substantially strengthens the empirical case beyond the main text.

The complementarity analysis and correlation between attention localization/entropy and classification contribution is an interesting post-hoc analysis that adds some interpretability value beyond pure accuracy numbers.
Combination of EP with LoRA (PEFT) demonstrating a dominant Pareto front is a nice practical finding showing EP is not simply redundant with fine-tuning.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited: EP is essentially a simplification of existing multi-query/multi-head cross-attention pooling (closely related to AbMILP generalized to M queries, and mathematically similar to MQCA/slot attention without iteration, GRU, or LayerNorm). The main contribution is removing a key-projection matrix that the authors themselves show is often redundant, which is an incremental engineering simplification rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Accuracy gains over strong existing attentive probing baselines (AIM, MHCA, CAE, CLIP-style pooling) are often very small (fractions of a percent in Figure 2/Table 2), with the main benefit being parameter/FLOP efficiency; for several strong backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP, SigLIP) EP's accuracy advantage over established methods is marginal, which tempers the significance of the central accuracy claim.

No code/artifact release is mentioned, and the experimental protocol involves a very large hyperparameter search (learning rate swept in [0.1, 5.0] per model/dataset with LARS, 90-epoch training, multiple D_o configurations), raising reproducibility concerns and the possibility that reported numbers benefit from extensive per-setting tuning not available to competing baselines in exactly the same way.

No error bars, variance across seeds, or significance testing are reported anywhere despite the numerous close comparisons (e.g., 0.1-0.5% accuracy differences are treated as meaningful in several tables/figures), making it hard to assess whether reported Pareto dominance is robust or within noise.

The scope is restricted to image classification (plus some zero-shot retrieval/localization as secondary probes); despite claiming localization and interpretability benefits, no segmentation or detection downstream evaluation is performed, which would be a more direct test of the claimed benefits of localized/complementary attention.

Several analyses (e.g., 'Comparison of pre-training methods' claims like 'MAE surpasses BYOL' or 'CAPI outperforms CLIP') are tangential to the paper's stated contribution and read as broader claims about representation learning that are not rigorously isolated from confounds such as architecture, data scale, and training recipe differences across the cited pre-trained checkpoints.

The complementarity metric and entropy-vs-accuracy correlation are presented as a notable 'emerging property,' but the analysis remains largely descriptive/correlational (as the authors themselves acknowledge in Limitations) without a controlled causal test (e.g., directly optimizing for complementarity shows only marginal gains in the auxiliary-loss experiment, undermining the practical significance of this finding).

The paper is very dense with a large number of near-duplicate scatter plots and tables (many nearly identical Pareto-front figures across datasets/backbones), which hurts clarity and makes it difficult for a reader to identify the single most important piece of evidence supporting the core claims.

strengths: Provides the first systematic, unifying framework (Table 1) that expresses a wide range of existing attentive pooling/probing methods (AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA, CLIP, CAiT, SigLIP, CoCa, CAE, DOLG) as instances of a common multi-head cross-attention formulation, clarifying their design choices and redundancies.

Derives a simple, well-motivated and genuinely lightweight method (Efficient Probing, EP) by algebraically absorbing redundant projection matrices, yielding large parameter/FLOP reductions while matching or exceeding state-of-the-art accuracy.

Extremely broad and thorough empirical evaluation: multiple datasets (ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-100, Places365, FGVC-Aircraft, Stanford Cars, CUB-200, Food-101), many pre-training paradigms and backbones (MIM: MAE/BEiTv2/SimMIM/CAPI; JEA: BYOL/DINO; hybrid: iBOT/DINOv2/DINOv3/Franca; VLM: CLIP/SigLIP/SigLIP2; generative: DiT/AIMv2), and model sizes from ViT-S to ViT-L/XL.

Rich set of complementary analyses beyond top-line accuracy: accuracy-vs-parameters and accuracy-vs-FLOPs Pareto curves, comparison and hybridization with PEFT methods (LoRA, BitFit, LayerNorm tuning), layer-wise and low-shot probing, in-/out-of-domain k-NN transfer, unsupervised object localization, zero-shot image retrieval, attention entropy/localization correlation with accuracy, attention complementarity metrics, Matryoshka-style multi-scale probing, and extensive qualitative attention visualizations.

The finding that EP's independent queries learn diverse, complementary, foreground-focused attention (rather than shortcut/background cues) and that this correlates with accuracy gains is an interesting and potentially impactful insight for interpretability and robustness.
The hybrid LoRA+EP results, showing a strictly dominant accuracy-parameter trade-off over either method alone, is a useful and non-trivial practical finding.
Clear writing, good figures, and an appendix that substantially extends the main results, improving reproducibility and credibility of the claims.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty of EP is somewhat incremental: it mainly amounts to algebraically absorbing the key projection into learnable queries for the multi-query case, extending an identity already noted for the single-query AbMILP case; the theoretical justification for why this absorption is harmless for M=1 but not in general when W_K is naively removed (Sec. 3.2) is argued mostly empirically rather than rigorously.

PEFT comparison (Figure 4, LoRA sweep) is conducted only on a single backbone/dataset (MAE ViT-B/16, ImageNet-1K); it is unclear whether the EP+LoRA complementarity finding generalizes to other pre-training paradigms (e.g., VLMs, generative models) studied elsewhere in the paper.

Most reported numbers appear to come from single runs without error bars, variance across seeds, or significance testing, making it hard to assess whether some of the smaller reported gains (e.g., attention-similarity loss, Matryoshka deltas, some Table 2 gains) are statistically meaningful.

Evaluation is restricted to classification-style transfer (plus retrieval and WSOL as secondary probes) on frozen features; the claimed benefits of complementary, localized attention are not tested on dense prediction tasks such as segmentation or detection, where patch-level representations would be most directly relevant.

The proposed complementarity and localization metrics are heuristic (cosine similarity of attention maps, attention mass within bounding boxes) and not validated against human judgments or established interpretability benchmarks, so claims about EP's improved interpretability remain only loosely substantiated.

Some ablations/novel extensions (attention mixing, Matryoshka probing) are explored but ultimately shown to be ineffective or only exploratory, slightly diluting the paper's focus and leaving these directions underdeveloped.

The paper explicitly limits scope to frozen backbones and acknowledges (Appendix D) that interactions between EP and more general fine-tuning/adapter strategies, as well as extension to non-classification tasks, remain open, somewhat narrowing the immediate scope of the contribution.
